name: Citicoline (CDP-choline)

lead: Citicoline is a naturally occurring nucleotide that supplies choline and cytidine for membrane synthesis. It is sold as a supplement in the US and used as a drug in some countries for stroke and cognitive decline. People take it as a nootropic for focus and memory.

After ingestion it is broken down into choline and cytidine, which the brain uses to make phosphatidylcholine, a membrane phospholipid. Pooled analyses of earlier trials suggested benefit in stroke, while the large ICTUS and COBRIT trials did not show overall benefit in stroke or brain injury. No trial tests it for appearance.

paras: It is taken orally as a supplement, usually as part of a nootropic or brain-health routine.
Grokipedia describes a good safety profile at therapeutic amounts.

angle.text: Citicoline supplies choline for brain cell membranes and is taken as a nootropic for focus and memory, aimed at better mental performance. It has been studied for stroke and brain injury.

lead: Citicoline, or cytidine 5'-diphosphocholine (CDP-choline), is a nucleotide that occurs naturally in the body as an intermediate in making phosphatidylcholine, a major membrane phospholipid.[1][2][3] It is sold as a prescription drug in some countries for stroke and cognitive disorders and as a dietary supplement in others, including the United States, where it is available over the counter, and it is marketed in more than 70 countries under names such as Cognizin, Somazina and Neurocoline.[1][3]

Its place in looksmaxxing and physique circles is as a cholinergic nootropic: people use it for focus, mental drive and training-session concentration, which they fold into the wider goal of working harder on diet, training and routine. On the T Nation forum it appears in nootropic stacks, eye-health discussions and dopamine threads, and some posters recommend it as a widely available choline source.[4][5][6]

Large randomised trials in acute ischaemic stroke and traumatic brain injury, notably ICTUS and COBRIT, did not show the benefit seen in earlier smaller studies, while pooled analyses of earlier trials had suggested one.[7][8][9] Smaller trials have looked at memory in healthy older adults, attention in adolescents and children, and visual function in optic nerve disease.[10][11][12] No published trial has tested citicoline for an appearance outcome.
infobox: About 1 hour after oral intake; choline about 4 hours

paras: Grokipedia reports approval for acute ischaemic stroke in Japan and several European countries but not as a US prescription drug.[1] Citicoline has been studied in ischaemic stroke, traumatic brain injury, vascular cognitive impairment, optic neuropathies and glaucoma, and substance dependence.[7][13][8][9][14][15][16][17][18] Studies in glaucoma suggest a possible protective effect on vision, according to Wikipedia.[3]

Citicoline is sold as a focus and memory supplement and is often combined with other nootropics. A T Nation poster described a daily stack that included citicoline, choline, DMAE, phosphatidylserine, pregnenolone and vinpocetine, and others discuss it alongside CILTEP-style combinations with ALCAR, caffeine and theanine.[5][19] Members of forum threads have asked how it compares with centrophenoxine and Alpha-GPC.[4][20]

Citicoline is an intermediate in the Kennedy pathway, in which choline is converted to phosphorylcholine and then to citicoline, which combines with diacylglycerol to form phosphatidylcholine.[3] A 1995 review described its metabolism and actions as an endogenous compound and when given exogenously.[2] Proposed benefits include neuroprotection after ischaemia and support for acetylcholine production.[3]

It is water-soluble with oral bioavailability above 90 percent. In the intestine it is hydrolysed to choline and cytidine, which cross the blood-brain barrier and are reassembled into citicoline in the brain. Plasma levels peak about one hour after oral intake and choline about four hours after. Most of the compound is eliminated as carbon dioxide in breath, with the remainder in urine.[3]
Wikipedia describes very low toxicity in animals and humans, with 2,000 mg per day studied and approved clinically; minor, transient effects such as stomach pain and diarrhea are rare.[3]

Citicoline entered clinical use as a prescription drug in the 1970s, mainly in Europe and Japan, for neurological conditions, according to Grokipedia, and approvals for acute ischaemic stroke exist in Japan and several European countries.[1] In the United States it has not been approved as a prescription drug for these uses and is instead sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement, a status Wikipedia also records.[1][3] Wikipedia lists a long run of trade names used in different markets, among them Ceraxon, Cognizin, Somazina, Neurocoline, Sinkron and Startonyl, and says citicoline is sold in more than 70 countries.[3]

Grokipedia reports that in 2025 the European Union declined to authorise health claims linking citicoline to cognitive benefits, citing insufficient evidence; that account is AI-generated and its details have not been independently confirmed here.[1] A 1998 review of neuroprotective therapy listed CDP-choline among ten classes of agents that had reached phase III trials in stroke with mixed results,[21] and a 2002 review described citicoline as a membrane stabiliser, reflecting the mechanism most often cited for its proposed benefit.[22]

In acute ischaemic stroke, the 2000 diffusion-weighted MRI study enrolled patients within 24 hours of symptom onset with moderate-to-severe deficits (NIHSS of 5 or higher) and examined whether citicoline changed the growth of the ischaemic lesion compared with placebo.[13] A phase III randomised trial of 2,000 mg published in Neurology in 2001 tested a high oral dose,[14] and the authors of a 2002 individual-patient pooling analysis noted that citicoline had been studied in many trials with positive findings but that only one had reached significance on its primary outcome; the pooled analysis evaluated oral citicoline on a combined recovery end point.[8] The international ICTUS trial, published in The Lancet in 2012 with 2,298 patients, set out to confirm efficacy in moderate-to-severe stroke and did not find an overall benefit; Wikipedia adds that a meta-analysis of seven trials reported no statistically significant long-term benefit for survival or recovery.[7][3]

In traumatic brain injury, the COBRIT trial (registered as NCT00545662) randomised 1,213 patients and, in its 2012 JAMA report, found no improvement in functional and cognitive status with citicoline compared with placebo.[9][23] A 2017 pharmacotherapy review for vascular cognitive impairment also covers citicoline.[15]

A 2020 systematic review of 47 articles on neurological use concluded that citicoline appeared useful for slowing dementia progression and improving stroke prognosis, while describing its effect after brain trauma as unclear.[24] A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis pooled studies in mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease and post-stroke dementia: all seven included studies reported a positive effect on cognition, and the pooled standardised mean differences ranged from 0.56 to 1.57 across sensitivity analyses, although the authors described the overall quality of the studies as poor.[25] A 2022 pharmacological and clinical review of stroke, brain injury and cognitive impairment updated an earlier 2016 review with 176 new references.[26]

In people without neurological disease, a randomised, double-blind trial examined memory in healthy older adults,[10] and a trial in 75 healthy adolescent males compared 250 or 500 mg of citicoline with placebo over 28 days on measures of attention, finger-tapping speed and impulsivity.[11] A 2024 randomised pilot study examined citicoline in children with ADHD.[12] Registered trials have also studied citicoline in non-arteritic ischaemic optic neuropathy, visual pathway conduction in optic nerve disease, methamphetamine dependence and alcohol dependence, and a phase 2 trial that began in 2026 is testing it for preventing cognitive decline after delirium.[16][17][18][27][28] No published trial has tested citicoline for an appearance outcome.

Citicoline is sold as a nootropic supplement in the US and EU.[1] On T Nation, posters describe it as a widely available choline source, some report mild mood effects or a dopamine-supporting role, and others list it among eye-health supplements citing glaucoma studies.[4][6][29] One user reported brain fog after stopping a stack of supplements that included it.[20]

Commercial products built around branded citicoline continue to launch; a 2026 press release from one supplement company announced a brain-health system built on the Cognizin brand of citicoline at a dose it described as clinically studied. A review of choline supplements published in 2023 grouped citicoline with alpha-GPC, choline bitartrate and lecithin as cholinergic compounds and acetylcholine precursors that are widely used as food supplements and that the authors described as a strategy for supporting memory and cognitive function.[30]

In training and self-improvement forums, citicoline is typically discussed as one component of a broader nootropic routine rather than a standalone product. The T Nation threads span more than two decades, from a 2001 poster listing a multi-ingredient daily stack to later discussions of CILTEP-style combinations, and the questions asked most often concern how it compares with Alpha-GPC or centrophenoxine.[4][20][5][19] No community source claims a direct change in appearance; the stated goal is focus and drive for study and training.

lore.intro: On T Nation, citicoline is discussed as a choline source and ingredient in nootropic stacks, with side threads on mood and eye health.[4][5][6]
